title: Why Nuclear Energy Is Making a Global Comeback | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Nuclear energy is experiencing its biggest global resurgence in decades, driven by energy-security fears from the Ukraine and Iran wars, climate goals, and AI-driven electricity demand -- but CFR experts stress the binding constraint is not technology or public opinion but the economics of building new plants on time and on budget, a feat achieved only in China, Russia, and South Korea over the last twenty years.

themes.theme: Scale and trajectory of the nuclear buildout

insights.claim: As of 2024 there are 417 nuclear power reactors operating across 31 countries, supplying roughly 9 percent of the world's electricity, according to the IAEA, with dozens more reactors under construction.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: A 9% global electricity share with dozens of reactors under construction gives a concrete baseline for sizing the nuclear buildout opportunity across uranium mining, reactor construction, and grid infrastructure.

insights.claim: In a high-case IAEA scenario, global nuclear capacity nearly triples by 2050, from 377 gigawatts to 992 gigawatts; in a low-case projection it still rises by about 50 percent.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: Even the IAEA's conservative case implies a 50% capacity expansion by 2050 -- a multi-decade demand tailwind for uranium miners, reactor OEMs, and grid-scale construction firms.

insights.claim: More than twenty countries committed in 2023 to tripling global nuclear energy capacity by 2050, a pledge CFR frames as the point the current comeback gained significant momentum.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: A multilateral 2023 tripling pledge is a policy anchor point that governments and utilities can be held to when assessing whether nuclear buildout commitments are being met.
insights.locator: 'Why is nuclear energy making a global comeback?' section

insights.claim: Vijay Vaitheeswaran, CFR's senior fellow and director of the Energy and Climate Program, called the current period 'the brightest moment for nuclear power globally in a couple of decades,' contingent on the challenging economics of new plants being overcome.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: The expert's own framing conditions the bullish nuclear narrative on solving plant economics -- the article's throughline that investors should treat as the key swing factor rather than assuming momentum alone guarantees delivery.
insights.quote: This is the brightest moment for nuclear power globally in a couple of decades.

insights.claim: Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine exposed Europe's dependence on Russian natural gas, and the 2026 Iran war has significantly disrupted global oil and gas markets, both accelerating governments' push toward nuclear energy for diversification even though the underlying nuclear push predates the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: Energy-security shocks from two separate wars are compounding to accelerate nuclear investment timelines globally -- a durable macro tailwind independent of either conflict's resolution.

insights.claim: The U.S. recently signed a thirty-year civil nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia (not yet in effect as of publication), which experts say weakens the nonproliferation norms set by the 2009 U.S.-UAE civil nuclear deal widely considered the 'gold standard.'
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: A weakened nonproliferation template with Saudi Arabia could become the new baseline for future U.S. civil nuclear deals in the Gulf, raising proliferation risk premiums for regional security analysis.
insights.locator: opening paragraph and 'Is nuclear energy safe?' section

insights.claim: CFR's Vaitheeswaran said the U.S.-Saudi nuclear deal, as declared, 'does represent a shift in policy for the United States—and from the point of proliferation, not necessarily a good one.'
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: An on-record CFR expert critique of the Saudi deal signals likely continued nonproliferation-community pushback and possible congressional scrutiny of the agreement before it takes effect.
insights.quote: Certainly the [U.S.-Saudi] agreement, as declared, does represent a shift in policy for the United States—and from the point of proliferation, not necessarily a good one.

themes.theme: AI power demand as a new nuclear driver

insights.claim: Data centers accounted for roughly 50 percent of total U.S. electricity demand growth in 2025, according to the International Energy Agency, making nuclear energy an increasingly favored solution to the AI-driven strain on electrical grids.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: A 50% AI-driven share of U.S. electricity demand growth is a hard number for sizing the nuclear-for-AI investment thesis and for forecasting incremental power demand from hyperscalers.

insights.claim: Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft have each signed at least one nuclear energy deal in 2026, a shift from their prior role as the main force behind U.S. clean energy development through wind and solar power purchase agreements.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: Big Tech's pivot from wind/solar PPAs to nuclear deals is a direct, trackable capital-allocation signal for power-sector investors and a leading indicator of hyperscaler energy strategy going forward.

themes.theme: Who leads nuclear production today and tomorrow

insights.claim: Just five countries -- the United States, China, France, Russia, and South Korea -- produce more than 70 percent of the world's nuclear electricity generation capacity, with the U.S. alone accounting for about 30 percent of global nuclear generation.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: A concentrated five-country production base means global nuclear supply-chain and policy risk is disproportionately tied to these markets' domestic politics and construction track records.
insights.locator: 'Which countries use the most nuclear energy?' section

insights.claim: The Trump administration aims to quadruple U.S. nuclear capacity from 100 GW to 400 GW by 2050, plans to expedite construction of ten large-scale commercial reactors by up to three years (complete designs under construction by 2030), and wants to encourage more small modular reactors.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: A 4x U.S. nuclear capacity target by 2050, with a concrete 2030 milestone for ten reactor designs, gives investors a specific policy target and timeline to track for execution risk.
insights.locator: 'Which countries use the most nuclear energy?' section

insights.claim: CFR's David Hart is skeptical the U.S. plan is achievable as designed: 'The administration wants to do everything all at once. I don't think they can,' arguing the U.S. instead needs to concentrate on a small number of reactor designs and build many of them.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: A CFR expert directly disputes the feasibility of the administration's 100-to-400-GW target, suggesting investors should discount the headline 2050 goal and instead watch for reactor-design standardization as the real signal of execution progress.
insights.quote: The administration wants to do everything all at once. I don't think they can. I think we really need to concentrate on a small number of designs and try to build a bunch of them, and I don't quite see that happening in our current policy.
insights.locator: 'Which countries use the most nuclear energy?' section

insights.claim: China is leading the world in new nuclear construction with nearly forty reactors currently under construction and aims to surpass the United States as the world's leader in nuclear capacity, with nuclear positioned as a pillar of China's energy strategy alongside its existing clean-energy edge.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: China's ~40-reactor construction pipeline is the single largest near-term driver of global nuclear capacity growth and a direct competitive threat to U.S. nuclear industry leadership claims.
insights.locator: 'Which countries use the most nuclear energy?' section

insights.claim: France generates roughly 70 percent of its electricity from nuclear power, the highest share of any country in the world, and is leading Europe's nuclear revival alongside Hungary and Slovakia, which are also expanding domestic nuclear capacity.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: France's 70% nuclear share is the reference case for a fully decarbonized grid built on nuclear baseload, and its European Union classification of nuclear as a climate-friendly investment (2022 law) underpins further EU nuclear expansion.
insights.locator: 'Which countries use the most nuclear energy?' section

themes.theme: The real constraint: economics, not technology or public opinion

insights.claim: No new nuclear plant has been built on time and on budget outside of China, Russia, or South Korea in the last twenty years, and development in the United States and Europe has been 'an utter disaster,' according to Vaitheeswaran, who called this the biggest obstacle to the nuclear resurgence.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: This is the article's central risk flag: bullish nuclear demand narratives (AI, energy security, climate) will not translate into delivered capacity in the U.S./Europe unless construction cost and schedule overruns are solved -- a key filter for evaluating any Western nuclear-buildout investment thesis.
insights.quote: In the early days of the industry, boosters claimed that nuclear power would be 'too cheap to meter.' Today, unless innovative policies and technologies produce nuclear power faster and cheaper than in the recent past, nuclear will be remembered as too costly to matter.

insights.claim: Nuclear reactors can operate for approximately eighty years, giving nuclear power a long-term baseload advantage over wind and solar, which require battery storage technology to provide reliable round-the-clock grid power.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: An 80-year operating lifespan materially changes the levelized cost-of-capital calculus for nuclear versus renewables-plus-storage, a key input for long-duration power infrastructure investment models.
insights.locator: 'Is nuclear energy clean and renewable?' section

insights.claim: Building nuclear power plants in or near conflict zones carries additional safety risk, as demonstrated by fears surrounding Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, which has been heavily targeted by Russia during the war, according to CFR expert Erin Dumbacher.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: Conflict-zone nuclear risk is a distinct underwriting factor for insurers and governments considering nuclear buildouts in geopolitically unstable regions.

insights.claim: More than 70 percent of respondents in a 2025 Bisconti Research survey said they favored using nuclear energy in the United States, and Gallup polling shows American support for nuclear energy has grown over the past decade -- a reversal from the stagnation of the 1980s and 1990s after disasters like Chernobyl.
insights.speaker: Roxy Ekberg
insights.so_what: Public opinion is no longer the binding constraint on U.S. nuclear expansion, shifting the entire policy debate toward financing and construction execution as the real bottleneck.
